blocks.text: But she who is born of the bee is well versed in household management and knows how to work. Hence in Xenophon's Oeconomicus, chapter 13, ἡ τῶν μελισσῶν ἡγεμῶν [hē tōn melissōn hēgemōn], the leader of the bees, is compared at length with the mother of a household. Accordingly, even illustrious women did not disdain to be called by the name of bee: as among the Hebrews there are two named DEBORA: one, the nurse of Rebecca, Gen. XXXV, 8, and the other, the prophetess who judged Israel, Iudicum IV, 4. And among the Greeks there is MELISSA, the nymph who nursed Jupiter; and MELISSA, daughter of Epidamnus, of whom Stephanus speaks under Δυῤῥάχιον [Dyrrhachion]; and MELISSA, wife of Periander, king of the Corinthians; and a later MELISSA, whose Letter Aldus published in the volume of Greek Letters. 4. It is also an accepted usage that the bee is called ἐργάτις [ergatis], craftswoman or worker. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 40: Εἰσὶ δ᾽ αἱ μικραὶ ἐργάτιδες μᾶλλον τῶν μεγάλων [Eisi d' hai mikrai ergatides mallon tōn megalōn]. Similar to this is Varro, Rustica, book 3, chapter 16: The wild ones are smaller in size, and hairy, but better workers. And in Anthologia, book 1, chapter 60, bees are called in Antiphilus

Αἰθερίου πτηναὶ νέκταρος ἐργάτιδες [Aitheriou ptēnai nektaros ergatides], winged craftswomen of heavenly nectar. [III, 369] Not to mention Lucian, who in the Halcyon calls the bee μέλιτος ἐργάτιν [melitos ergatin], as also Pisides calls her τὴν σοφὴν τὴν ἐργάτιν [tēn sophēn tēn ergatin]. 5. But no one else, so far as I know, has called their ἐργασίαν σεμνὴν [ergasian semnēn]. Ambrose renders this venerable operation, Jerome chaste work, Castalio august work, Godefridus Tilmannus work full of cleanliness and honesty. I would prefer precious work or wonderful work, because it fits the matter better; and the old lexicographers teach that σεμνὸν [semnon] or σεπτὸν [septon] is taken in this sense. Hesychius: Σεμνή· (read Σεμνὰ) τίμια, σώφρων [Semnē (Semna): timia, sōphrōn]. The same: Σεπτά· θαυμαστά [Septa: thaumasta]. Following this, the Arabic version here has that the bee makes her work عجيبة طرفة [ʿajība ṭurfa], with wonderful art. (Wrongly printed طرقة [ṭrqa].) What if one were to read σμήνων [smēnōn] for σεμνὴν [semnēn], thus: τήν τε ἐργασίαν σμήνων ὡς ποιεῖται [tēn te ergasian smēnōn hōs poieitai], and how she does the work of the hives, that is, that wonderful work which is done in hives? This is a great secret of nature, and not yet sufficiently understood. The Philosopher, in the place cited above: Ὅταν δὲ εἰς σμῆνος ἀφίκωνται ἀποσείονται, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσιν ἑκάστῃ τρεῖς, ἢ τέτταρες. τὸ δὲ λαμβανόμενον οὐ ῥᾴδιόν ἐστιν ἰδεῖν, οὐδὲ τὴν ἐργασίαν, ὅν τινα τρόπον ποιοῦνται, οὐκ ὦπται· [Hotan de eis smēnos aphikōntai aposeiontai, kai akolouthousin hekastē treis, ē tettares. to de lambanomenon ou rhadion estin idein, oude tēn ergasian, hon tina tropon poiountai, ouk ōptai] When they return to the hive (from gathering flowers), they shake themselves off, and each bee is followed by three or four. But what they receive is not easy to see. Nor has it yet been observed how they do their work. Worth knowing, if only it is true, is what Alkazuinius and Damir report about this, [col. 514] وقد صنع ارسطاطاليس لها بيتا من زجاج لينظر الي كيفية ما تصنع فابت ان تعمل حتي لطخته من باطن الزجاج بالطين [wa-qad ṣanaʿa Arisṭāṭālīs lahā baytan min zujāj li-yanẓura ilā kayfiyyat mā taṣnaʿ fa-abat an taʿmal ḥattā laṭṭakhathu min bāṭin al-zujāj bi-l-ṭīn] Aristotle made them a glass hive, in order to look in and see how they set about their work. But they refused to do any work until they had smeared the inside of the glass with mud. 6. There follows in the sacred text: Ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται· [Hēs tous ponous basileis kai idiōtai pros hygieian prospherontai] whose labours kings and private persons use for health. The labours of the bee, that is, honey: as in Hesiod's well-known line on drones, Works, line 303.
Οἵ τε μελισσάων κάματον τρύχουσιν ἀεργοὶ, [Hoi te melissaōn kamaton trychousin aergoi]
And who, idle, consume the labour of the bees. And in Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris, there is reckoned among the funeral offerings

the labour of the tawny bees. Hence the proverb about a young man who wastes time uselessly explaining something commonly known: Σύγγνωθι τῷ μειρακίῳ τὸ μέλι πόνον μελίττης κηρύττοντι [Syngnōthi tō meirakiō to meli ponon melittēs kēryttonti], Forgive the young man who proclaims that honey is the labour of the bee. On this, Tzetzes, Chiliad 8, History 208: [III, 370] Τοῦτο τὸ σχῆμα γίνωσκε τυγχάνειν εἰρωνείας. Καὶ τίς γὰρ, ὃς ἠγνόηκε πόνον μελίσσης μέλι; [Touto to schēma ginōske tynchanein eirōneias. Kai tis gar, hos ēgnoēke ponon melissēs meli?]
